title: Crafted by Curiosity
description: A reflection on how children’s creativity, persistence, and love for hands-on learning reveal something deeply human. From crochet to glitter-covered chargers, their willingness to keep improving shows that growth comes through practice, challenge, and imperfect attempts—and that in an age of AI, skills built through our own hands, patience, and experience still hold unique value.
full_description:
My elder daughter picked up crocheting a few weeks back and she's glued to it. Meanwhile, my younger daughter discovered her own canvas. Every charger in the house or glasses. Glittery beads, glue and whatever design inspires her that day transform chargers into her art project, one dazzling layer at a time.

What struck me most is that neither of them stopped at good enough (or it seems). My elder daughter progressed beyond basic stitches into designs / art work within weeks. My younger one continually upgrades her art, adding more sparkle, detail and her own unique touch. They’re driven by the challenge itself.

There’s a psychological explanation for this. Research on motivation reveals that achieving a goal triggers a reward in the brain. This reward not only feels good but also motivates us to seek out more difficult challenges. Success or meeting your goal doesn’t lead to complacency; it pushes us to grow and stretch.

Watching them transition from let me try this to look what I made prompted me to think and write about this.

They manage all this alongside school and hifz; Alhmadulillah, memorising the Qur’an, keeping up with their studies and still finding time for yarn, glue and glitter. Both fought for this time and learned something few classrooms teach these days. How to build something with your hands, imperfectly at first, then improving and ultimately creating something beautiful.

This brings me to a larger perspective. Our mothers and grandmothers were skilled in handcrafts such as crochet, sewing and cooking. We were instead drawn into classrooms, where school became the AI of our generation, standardising skills that had been passed down through families. Decades later, the very thing that replaced our grandmothers’ skills (education, structured knowledge, schools) is being replaced by actual AI

Crochet, carpentry, plumbing and even a glitter-covered charger; these still belong to us. It’s not because AI can’t eventually master them but because they’re built on something slower: dexterity and muscle memory honed through countless imperfect attempts. My daughters aren’t simply decorating yarn and chargers. They’re demonstrating that the drive to grow and strive for greater heights remains theirs to experience and achieve.

title: Overthinking in business
description:
Things I used to overthink as a business owner… that don’t carry the same weight anymore.

How will clients come? How will we sustain expenses?

At the beginning, these questions felt heavy. Almost like they needed to be answered completely before taking a single step.

But now, looking back, I realize something deeper:
We were never fully in control of those answers to begin with.
full_description:
I've been reflecting on this thought lately:

Destiny doesn't reveal itself all at once. It reveals itself only to those who have the patience to keep walking.

When people hear the word sabr, they often imagine waiting.

Doing nothing.
Enduring until life changes.
But I see patience differently.

Patience is not the absence of action. It is continuing to act when the outcome refuses to reveal itself. When we started TRPL Solutions there was a project we almost didn't take. It was bigger than anything we had built before.

We questioned ourselves. Were we ready? Did we have enough experience? Could we actually deliver?

Confidence said, "Not yet."
Tawakkul said, "Take the next step."

So we did. Not because we knew how everything would unfold.

But because we believed that our responsibility was the effort, not the outcome. Months later, that same project is nearing completion.

Looking back, I don't think confidence came before the journey. The journey gave me confidence. That seems to be how Allah teaches us. The path rarely becomes visible before we begin walking. It reveals itself one step at a time.

The same is true with people. Clients sometimes delay payments because they're carrying burdens you cannot see. Colleagues make mistakes while fighting battles they never speak about.

Sometimes the easiest response is to react. To replace. To walk away.

But I've learned that patience is also a form of belief. Belief that people can grow. Belief that trust, once invested wisely, often bears fruit later than expected.

Without tawakkul, patience feels like carrying a weight. With tawakkul, patience is a strategy.

You stop demanding that life explain itself immediately. You begin trusting that some answers only arrive with time.

Perhaps that is why so much of life only makes sense in retrospect.

The delays.
The disappointments.
The unexpected turns.

None of them seemed meaningful while they were happening. Yet looking back, they formed a path I could never have designed myself.

Maybe destiny is not something we discover at the end. Maybe it is something that quietly reveals itself to those who refuse to stop walking.

And perhaps that is what patience has been all along.

title: What truly drives performance
description: In business, we rely heavily on numbers: revenue targets, utilisation rates, margins, cashflow, cost controls etc.. In our business of IT enabled products, we engineer entire systems around measurement. Numbers give direction. Money provides fuel. Without them, organisations cannot survive, let alone grow. However, observing around I realised that two busineses may have similar credentials, tools, and frameworks.

title: Between momentum & meaning
description: Business is growing, responsibility has increased, and there’s clarity of purpose (or it seems). There’s a quiet sense of contentment in that. And yet, alongside it, there’s also conflict. Not the kind of conflict driven by fear or instability. This is a different tension, one between momentum and meaning.
full_description:
Between momentum & meaning

Business is growing, responsibility has increased, and there’s clarity of purpose (or it seems). There’s a quiet sense of contentment in that. And yet, alongside it, there’s also conflict. Not the kind of conflict driven by fear or instability. This is a different tension, one between momentum and meaning.

Over the years I have become more aware of how growth changes everything. Responsibility deepens, and with it comes the weight of knowing that your choices now affect more lives than just your own.

What I didn’t expect was how easily speed begins to crowd out depth. Not through bad intentions, but through small, reasonable compromises made in the name of efficiency. That’s when I started feeling unsure, not about direction, but about growth.

What worries me isn’t failure. It’s the possibility of success that quietly erodes the very values that made the journey meaningful in the first place. The fear that growth, if left unchecked, can dilute quality, thoughtfulness, honesty, and presence (or is success even success without values or meaning?).

Stability comes with its own questions. What do you optimise for when fear or need is no longer driving you? That’s where integrity is really tested, not in hardship, but in momentum.

I’m learning that responsibility isn’t about carrying everything. It’s about deciding what must not be compromised as complexity grows. Protecting quality when speed is rewarded. Protecting truth when silence is easier. Protecting people around you.

I don’t have this fully figured out yet. I’m still learning where to pause and where to push, how to lead without being consumed, how to grow without becoming someone I wouldn’t want to work for.

But one thing feels increasingly clear a business can grow faster than the inner life of the person leading it and that gap if left unchecked is dangerous and is often recognised only when its too late.

Right now, my focus isn’t only on scaling systems or revenue. It’s on scaling without losing alignment with values, with clarity, with the reasons I started at all.

title: Your rizq is already written for you
description:
Your rizq is already written for you, and Allah will never abandon you.

I founded my software company last year, and it has been about 13 months of building since then. And I’ve slowly started to internalize is this. We were never meant to carry the burden of how our provision will come because that was never in our control to begin with.

title: Children grow up fast
description:
I remember my eldest daughter being born with remarkable clarity. I can still picture every little detail. The tiny person trying to make sense of a new world, looking around with curious eyes. 

She would fall asleep on my chest, and today she is almost as tall as I am.

title: Reputation is everything
description:
Revenue is important but reputation is everything. In the beginning, revenue seems to be the primary driving force in business. 

More clients. More projects. More growth.

title: Importance of building systems for founders
description:
Passion might build things and give you a good start but systems sustain them.

In the beginning, I believed passion and hard work could compensate for almost anything. And to some extent, they can. When you're small, energy hides inefficiency. You work longer hours, respond faster, and carry more yourself.

title: Character
description: True character of a team isn’t revealed when everything goes according to plan; it’s revealed when almost nothing does.

title: Raising children
description: I am raising my 2 children differently. People tell me my approach is wrong. They go to school while doing Hifz. The modern world often makes it feel like you must choose.  And somewhere along the way, we accepted the idea that raising children must become a choice between dunya and deen making them mutually exclusive.

title: The biggest lesson I learned in building my company
description: We didn’t ignore preparation entirely. In many ways, we did what any finance-oriented founder would do. We built feasibility studies, projections, and market studies.
full_description:
The biggest lesson I learned in the first 3 months of building my company

Not what you might expect.

Not a bad product, neither the wrong timing nor a difficult market.

We didn’t ignore preparation entirely. In many ways, we did what any finance-oriented founder would do. We built feasibility studies, projections, and market studies.

On paper, we were good to go. But we missed the part that mattered most. Structure.

I hired developers. Only developers. The best I could.

When you believe in an idea deeply enough, there’s a quiet pull to just begin. To build. To move. That energy isn’t wrong.

But conviction without preparation is just enthusiasm with a timeline.

At the time, it seemed logical.

We were a software company, so naturally the focus went into building software. But I had confused the product with the foundation of the business itself.

A business isn’t only what it creates. It’s how it sells, how it supports its people, and how it thinks about tomorrow while delivering today.

The gap showed up quickly.

We had capability without structure. Technical depth without operational clarity. The ability to deliver, but not yet the foundation to grow.

What I didn’t fully understand then was this:

A team reflects the assumptions of its founder.

I assumed we would figure the rest out later. The team assumed the same. And for a while, momentum carried us forward until it no longer could.

10 months in, I’m still correcting that early imbalance. Slowly. Deliberately. One honest conversation and one right hire at a time.

The lesson isn’t that urgency was wrong.

It’s that urgency without enough homework doesn’t save time. It simply shifts the cost to a later stage, where it becomes heavier, harder, and far more personal.

The idea deserved more than excitement.

It deserved full attention before the first line of code was written.

title: Are customised softwares a thing of the past?
description: It’s undeniable that off-the-shelf software solutions can serve many businesses well, especially when quick setup and basic functionality are sufficient. However, when organizations seek real competitive advantage or need to address unique business challenges, customised software remains irreplaceable.
